It means Christ will return in the year 2000
If Christ may come for the church at any moment with no signs preceding, the rapture must precede the tribulation events

Walvoord and Thomas Ice argue that New Testament exhortations to watch (e.g. James 5:8-9; Titus 2:13) imply no prophesied event must come first; posttribulationists reply that watching is compatible with expected signs (Matthew 24:33).
What role does national Israel have in the dispensational millennium?
Israel is restored to its land and receives the fulfilment of its covenant promises, with Christ reigning from Jerusalem
Israel plays no distinct role, having been replaced by the church
Israel is judged and excluded
Israel's promises were fulfilled in the Maccabean era
Dispensationalists read the Abrahamic, Davidic and new covenant promises (e.g. Genesis 15; 2 Samuel 7; Jeremiah 31; Ezekiel 40-48) as including a literal national and territorial fulfilment.
Which of these rapture views is held by some premillennialists but is NOT the classic dispensational position?
The pretribulational view
The view that the rapture precedes Daniel's seventieth week
The prewrath view (rapture during the second half of the seventieth week, before God's wrath)
The view that the church is absent from Revelation 4-19

Marvin Rosenthal and Alan Kurschner developed the prewrath view; Gleason Archer argued a mid-seventieth-week rapture in Three Views on the Rapture (1984). Classic dispensationalism is pretribulational.
How does progressive dispensationalism (Blaising, Bock, Saucy, early 1990s) differ from earlier forms?
It abandons premillennialism for amillennialism
It sees more continuity, holding that Christ is already reigning in an inaugurated Davidic kingdom while still expecting a future for national Israel
It rejects any distinction between Israel and the church
It teaches that the rapture happened in AD 70

Craig Blaising and Darrell Bock's Progressive Dispensationalism (1993) and Robert Saucy's The Case for Progressive Dispensationalism (1993) present an 'already/not yet' Davidic reign; most remain pretribulational but some are less committed to it.
What does partial preterism hold?
Every prophecy, including the resurrection, was fulfilled by AD 70
No prophecy has yet been fulfilled
Many prophecies, including much of the Olivet Discourse and Revelation, were fulfilled in the events of AD 66-70, while the Second Coming, resurrection and final judgment remain future
Revelation outlines church history from Pentecost to the present
R. C. Sproul's The Last Days According to Jesus (1998), Kenneth Gentry and Gary DeMar defend this view; 'preterist' comes from Latin praeteritus, 'gone by'.
Which 'time texts' are central to partial preterist arguments?
Matthew 24:34, Matthew 16:28 and Revelation 1:1, 3 ('the time is near')
Genesis 1:1 and John 1:1
Daniel 12:2 and Revelation 20:12
Psalm 90:4 and 2 Peter 3:8

Preterists argue that 'this generation', 'some standing here' and 'what must soon take place' signal fulfilment within the first readers' lifetime; futurists reply that these may express certainty, prophetic perspective, or a future generation.
Which Counter-Reformation Jesuit is often credited with the first systematic preterist commentary on Revelation?
Manuel Lacunza
Robert Bellarmine
Luis de Alcázar (Vestigatio arcani sensus in Apocalypsi, 1614)

Alcázar read most of Revelation as fulfilled in the church's victories over Judaism and pagan Rome; Ribera's commentary pointed in the opposite, futurist direction. Earlier writers such as Eusebius also saw parts of the Olivet Discourse fulfilled in AD 70.
How does Gentry identify the beast's number 666 (Revelation 13:18)?
The Pope, through the Latin title Vicarius Filii Dei
Nero Caesar, whose name in Hebrew letters (Nrwn Qsr) totals 666
Muhammad
A future world ruler who has not yet appeared
Gentry also notes the variant reading 616, which matches the Latin spelling Nero Caesar, as supporting evidence; critics question whether Asian Gentile readers would compute a Hebrew spelling.
Why does the dating of Revelation matter so much for partial preterism?
Because a late date would prove dispensationalism
If Revelation was written before AD 70, its 'soon' prophecies can refer to the Jewish War; a c. AD 95 date makes AD 70 fulfilment of Revelation impossible
Because the date determines the author's identity
Because a pre-70 date would place Revelation before the Gospels in every case

Gentry's Before Jerusalem Fell argues for c. AD 65-66 from internal evidence such as the temple (Revelation 11:1-2) and the sixth king (17:10). Most scholars still favour the Domitianic date, so the question is disputed. Some preterists apply Revelation to Rome's fall instead.
How do partial preterists read 'the Son of Man coming on the clouds' in Matthew 24:30?
As the bodily Second Coming at the end of history only
As the pretribulational rapture
As a reference to Pentecost
As a judgment-coming against Jerusalem, echoing Old Testament cloud-comings of God in judgment (e.g. Isaiah 19:1) and Daniel 7:13's enthronement
N. T. Wright and Gentry read Daniel 7:13 as the Son of Man's vindication before the Ancient of Days. Many partial preterists then see a transition to the final coming at Matthew 24:36 or later.
Which ancient historian do partial preterists cite most often for the details of Jerusalem's fall?
Josephus (The Jewish War)
Herodotus
Thucydides
Bede

Josephus describes famine, false prophets, the siege and the temple's burning, which preterists match with Matthew 24 and Luke 21:20-24. Critics caution against reading Josephus's rhetoric too precisely.
What is the key difference between partial and full preterism?
Partial preterists date Revelation after AD 95
Full preterists deny that AD 70 had any prophetic significance
Partial preterists affirm a future bodily Second Coming, resurrection and final judgment; full preterists place all of these in the first century
Partial preterists reject the creeds

Partial preterists often cite Acts 1:11 and 1 Corinthians 15 for a future visible return and bodily resurrection, and several (e.g. Mathison's edited volume When Shall These Things Be?) have written critiques of full preterism.
With which millennial views is partial preterism commonly combined?
Only dispensational premillennialism
Only historicist premillennialism
None; it rejects all millennial views
Postmillennialism and amillennialism

Gentry and DeMar are postmillennial; many amillennialists, and Sproul (who did not commit firmly), accept preterist readings of the Olivet Discourse. The pairing with dispensational premillennialism is rare because dispensationalists place these prophecies in a future tribulation.
What does full preterism (also called 'consistent' or 'covenant eschatology') hold?
All biblical prophecy, including the Second Coming, resurrection and final judgment, was fulfilled by AD 70
The Second Coming is future but the tribulation is past
Revelation describes church history to the present
Most prophecy remains future
Advocates such as Max King (The Spirit of Prophecy, 1971; The Cross and the Parousia of Christ, 1987) and Don Preston argue that the time texts require a complete first-century fulfilment.
Why do critics say full preterism stands outside historic creedal orthodoxy?
It rejects the Trinity
It denies Christ's bodily resurrection on the third day
The ecumenical creeds confess a future return of Christ to judge and a future resurrection of the body, which full preterism places in the past
It teaches a pretribulational rapture

Critics such as Keith Mathison (ed., When Shall These Things Be?, 2004) argue this; proponents respond that creeds are subordinate to Scripture and that they affirm the return and resurrection as biblical events, though now fulfilled. Most full preterists affirm the Trinity and Christ's own bodily resurrection.
Which nineteenth-century book is often regarded as a precursor of modern full preterism?
Darby's Synopsis of the Books of the Bible
J. Stuart Russell's The Parousia (1878)
Elliott's Horae Apocalypticae
Hendriksen's More Than Conquerors

Russell, a Congregationalist minister, argued that every New Testament reference to the parousia pointed to the destruction of Jerusalem; the work was reprinted and became influential among later full preterists.
How do many full preterists, following Max King, understand the resurrection of 1 Corinthians 15?
As the resurrection of all bodies from their graves at a future date
As reincarnation
As a corporate, covenantal resurrection of the people of God from the old covenant into the new, completed in AD 70
As fulfilled only in the conversion of individual believers today

Some full preterists instead hold an individual view in which believers receive immortal bodies in heaven at death. Critics point to the bodily resurrection of Christ as 'firstfruits' (1 Corinthians 15:20-23) as requiring a like resurrection of believers' bodies.
Which text do critics cite as an apostolic warning relevant to full preterism?
2 Timothy 2:17-18, on Hymenaeus and Philetus saying the resurrection had already happened

Critics see a parallel with claiming a past resurrection; full preterists reply that the error lay in claiming completion before AD 70, not in claiming the resurrection would occur within that generation.
What is the core argument full preterists press against partial preterists?
That Revelation was written after AD 95
That the Gospels are unreliable
That the Olivet Discourse refers only to the end of the world
If the time texts limit the 'coming' in Matthew 24 to that generation, the same consistency should apply to other coming and resurrection texts

Full preterists argue that the Olivet Discourse is a single coming and that texts like Matthew 16:27-28 tie judgment to Jesus' generation. Partial preterists respond that Scripture speaks of more than one 'coming', and that texts like Acts 1:11 describe a visible, bodily return.
Which passage do critics stress as requiring a future, visible, bodily return?
Acts 1:11 (Jesus will come 'in the same way' as he was seen going into heaven)
Critics argue 'in the same way' implies a bodily, visible return; full preterists typically read it as a cloud-coming in judgment, comparable to Old Testament theophanies.
What do full preterists say about history after AD 70?
The world will end in a future tribulation
The kingdom is fully established and continues indefinitely, with the church living in the new covenant age without a future end-of-history event
History ended in AD 70 and nothing since is real
A future rapture is still expected

Most full preterists hold that human history continues without end and that believers enter heaven at death; critics see this as removing the Christian hope of bodily resurrection and new creation (Romans 8:18-23).
What does historicism hold about the book of Revelation?
It was entirely fulfilled by AD 70
It describes only the final seven years before Christ returns
It conveys timeless principles with no specific historical referents
It forecasts the course of church and world history from the apostolic age to Christ's return in sequence
Historicists read the seals, trumpets and bowls as successive eras of history; it was the dominant Protestant approach from the Reformation to the mid-nineteenth century.
What is the 'day-year principle'?
Prophetic days stand for years, so 1,260 days (Revelation 12:6) signify 1,260 years
Each day of creation lasted a thousand years
A day with the Lord is as a thousand years, so the millennium is a single day
Prophecies about days must be fulfilled within one year
Historicists appeal to Numbers 14:34 and Ezekiel 4:6, and to the seventy 'weeks' of Daniel 9 being weeks of years; critics argue these texts are specific instances rather than a general rule.
Whom did the Protestant Reformers and most historicists identify as the Antichrist or man of lawlessness?
A future Jewish world ruler
The papacy, understood as an office rather than a single individual
The Ottoman sultan alone

Luther, Calvin and many later Protestants held this; the original Westminster Confession (25.6) called the pope 'that Antichrist', a line later removed by several Presbyterian bodies. Many historicists also identified Islam with parts of the trumpet visions.
Which pair are notable English historicist interpreters of the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries?
John Nelson Darby and C. I. Scofield
Max King and Don Preston
William Hendriksen and Greg Beale
Joseph Mede and Isaac Newton

Mede's Clavis Apocalyptica (1627) and Newton's Observations upon the Prophecies of Daniel and the Apocalypse of St. John (published 1733) shaped later historicism; Mede also revived premillennial expectation among English Puritans.
Which nineteenth-century work is a monumental four-volume historicist commentary on Revelation?
E. B. Elliott's Horae Apocalypticae (1844)
Gentry's Before Jerusalem Fell
Pentecost's Things to Come
Wright's Jesus and the Victory of God
Elliott interpreted Revelation as a detailed chronology of church history; Albert Barnes's Notes also followed a historicist approach in America.
With which millennial views has historicism been combined?
Only full preterism
Both premillennialism and postmillennialism (and some amillennialism)
None; historicism has no view of the millennium

Mede was premillennial, many Puritans and Jonathan Edwards combined historicist exegesis with postmillennial hope, and Seventh-day Adventism today combines historicism with its own distinctive millennial view.
What is a common criticism of historicism, and how do historicists reply?
It ignores the Old Testament; they reply it uses only Daniel
Interpreters disagree widely and repeatedly identify their own era as the climax; historicists reply that the overall pattern of fulfilment is clear even if details are debated
It denies the Second Coming; they reply it is preterist
It requires a late date of Revelation; they reply with Gentry
Failed date-setting (for example, around 1844) damaged the approach's credibility; defenders argue that the identification of the papacy and the rise of Islam display real prophetic fulfilment.
Where is historicism still prominent today?
In dispensational seminaries such as Dallas
In the Roman Catholic magisterium
In Seventh-day Adventism and among some confessional Protestant writers
In all major evangelical study Bibles
Adventist prophetic interpretation (e.g. LeRoy Froom's The Prophetic Faith of Our Fathers) is historicist, and some Reformed and Presbyterian writers continue the Reformation tradition.
What does futurism hold about the book of Revelation?
Most of Revelation, typically chapters 4-22, describes events still future, clustered around Christ's return
Revelation was fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem
Revelation traces church history from the apostles to now
Revelation teaches only timeless principles
Futurism is held by dispensationalists (Walvoord, The Revelation of Jesus Christ, 1966) and in modified forms by many historic premillennialists such as Ladd.
What was Francisco Ribera's role in the history of futurism?
He invented the pretribulational rapture
He wrote the first preterist commentary
He founded the Plymouth Brethren
This Spanish Jesuit's commentary on Revelation (c. 1590) placed most of the book in a future period of three and a half years under a single Antichrist

Ribera's work is widely seen as a Counter-Reformation response to the Protestant identification of the papacy with Antichrist; futurists note that early writers such as Irenaeus and Hippolytus already expected a future Antichrist.
Who was Manuel Lacunza?
An Anglican bishop who devised the day-year principle
A Chilean Jesuit whose futurist premillennial work, published under the name 'Juan Josafat Ben-Ezra', was translated by Edward Irving in 1827
The editor of the Scofield Reference Bible
A Puritan who wrote the Savoy Declaration
The Coming of Messiah in Glory and Majesty influenced the British prophetic movement of the 1820s and 1830s, including circles around Irving and the Albury and Powerscourt conferences.
What do futurists claim about early church support?
The early church universally held the pretribulational rapture
Early writers such as Irenaeus and Hippolytus expected a future personal Antichrist and future tribulation before Christ's return
The early church read Revelation as fulfilled in AD 70
The early church never commented on Revelation
Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.25-30) and Hippolytus (On Christ and Antichrist) are cited as evidence that futurist elements are ancient, even though the full modern system developed later.
How does 'moderate' futurism differ from dispensational futurism?
Moderate futurists deny any future Second Coming
Moderate futurists date all of Revelation to AD 70
Moderate futurists use the day-year principle exclusively
Moderate futurists (e.g. Ladd) see the seals partly fulfilled through the church age and do not separate Israel and the church or posit a pretribulational rapture

Ladd's A Commentary on the Revelation of John (1972) mixes futurism with present-age application; dispensational futurism also reads the letters to the seven churches as foreshadowing church-age eras.
Why do some dispensational futurists regard Revelation 4:1 as significant?
The call 'come up here' and the absence of the word 'church' from chapters 4-19 are read as suggesting the church has been raptured
It gives the date of Revelation
It describes the binding of Satan
Critics note that John's ascent is personal and that 'saints' appear throughout chapters 4-19; dispensationalists reply that the saints in those chapters are tribulation converts.
What do futurists consider a major strength of their approach?
It requires the earliest possible date for Revelation
It identifies the Pope as Antichrist
It takes the cosmic scale of Revelation's judgments and the return of Christ (Revelation 19) at face value as events not yet seen in history
It removes the need for a future Second Coming

Futurists argue that worldwide judgments, a resurrection and the new creation have plainly not yet occurred; critics reply that the opening time texts (Revelation 1:1, 3; 22:10) imply relevance to the first readers.
How do futurists answer the objection that a mostly future Revelation would have been irrelevant to its first readers?
They concede the book was irrelevant to its first readers
They argue Revelation was written in the twentieth century
They claim the first readers lived during the tribulation
The letters to the churches addressed them directly, and the future victory of Christ gave them hope and exhortation to endure
Futurists add that 'soon' may express imminence or certainty from God's perspective (2 Peter 3:8), so the book remained relevant even if fulfilment was long delayed.
Idealism (the spiritual approach)
What does the idealist approach say Revelation primarily depicts?
The ongoing conflict between God and evil, Christ and Satan, throughout the whole church age, in symbolic form
A detailed chronology of world history
Events limited to AD 66-70
Only the last seven years before Christ returns
Idealists (also called the 'spiritual' or 'symbolic' approach) read the visions as recurring patterns applicable in every generation, culminating in Christ's final victory.
Which fourth-century North African exegete influenced Augustine toward a spiritual reading of Revelation?
Josephus
Tyconius, a Donatist, wrote a lost commentary and a book of interpretive rules; his symbolic approach shaped Augustine's City of God and much later Western exegesis.
Which book by William Hendriksen (1939) is a classic idealist-amillennial reading of Revelation?
The Blessed Hope
More Than Conquerors
Days of Vengeance
Things to Come
Hendriksen divided Revelation into seven parallel sections, each running from the first coming to the second; the method is called progressive parallelism.
What do idealists see as a strength of their approach?
It allows precise date-setting for Christ's return
It identifies Nero as the beast
It makes the book directly relevant to Christians in every era rather than to one generation only
It requires a literal thousand-year reign
Idealists argue that apocalyptic symbols communicate theological truths about persecution, false worship and perseverance applicable in every age.
What is a common critique of pure idealism, and the idealist reply?
That it detaches Revelation from concrete history; idealists reply that the symbols refer to real historical patterns and to a real final consummation
That it denies the Second Coming; they reply that it is premillennial
That it relies on a pre-70 date; they reply with Irenaeus
That it ignores Old Testament imagery; they reply it uses only Greek myths
Pure idealism without a historical anchor is rare; most idealists, like Hendriksen, affirm a literal final coming, resurrection and judgment.
Which nineteenth-century Scottish scholar is often cited as a classic idealist interpreter?
E. B. Elliott
John Walvoord
Milligan's lectures and commentary on Revelation (1880s) argued that the book sets forth principles rather than predicting particular events.
How does Greg Beale describe his own approach to Revelation?
Strict dispensational futurism
A 'redemptive-historical' or eclectic form of modified idealism that includes a future consummation
Strict historicism using the day-year principle

Beale's NIGTC commentary (1999) holds that the visions symbolise the church-age conflict but anticipate Christ's final coming and judgment, combining idealist with some futurist and preterist elements.
With which millennial view is idealism most often combined?
No millennial view has ever combined with it
Reading Revelation 20 as a symbolic picture of the present age fits amillennialism naturally; Warfield's postmillennialism also drew on a broadly idealist reading of Revelation 20.
What characterises the eclectic approach to Revelation?
It rejects all four classic approaches
It is identical to historicism
It applies only to Daniel
It combines elements of preterism, futurism and idealism, holding that the visions addressed first-century readers, apply to every age, and point to a future consummation
Scholars such as Greg Beale, Craig Keener and Grant Osborne combine approaches, arguing each captures part of the book's purpose.
Which reference work presents historicist, preterist, futurist and spiritual readings in parallel columns?
Steve Gregg's Revelation: Four Views
Clouse's The Meaning of the Millennium
Scofield's Reference Bible
Gregg's parallel commentary (1997; revised 2013) lets readers compare each approach verse by verse, and itself models an evenhanded, eclectic study.
How does Craig Keener's eclectic reading treat the first readers of Revelation?
He holds the book was irrelevant to its first readers
He reads it as a chronology of church history
He anchors the symbols in first-century Roman Asia while applying them to later believers and to the future return of Christ
He holds it was entirely fulfilled in AD 70
Keener's NIV Application Commentary on Revelation (2000) emphasises the imperial cult and persecution context while affirming a future consummation.
What do eclectic interpreters see as the strength of their method?
It eliminates every interpretive disagreement
It requires only one millennial view
It avoids the Old Testament entirely
It respects the book's first-century setting, its ongoing relevance, and its genuinely future hope together
Advocates argue Revelation itself combines letters to real churches, symbolic visions of recurring conflict, and prophecy of the end (Revelation 1:19 is sometimes read in this threefold way).
What is a common critique of the eclectic approach, and the reply?
That it can seem arbitrary in choosing which approach to apply; eclectics reply that genre, context and Old Testament allusion guide the choice
That it denies the Second Coming; they reply it is full preterist
That it is unknown to modern scholarship; they reply it is medieval
That it requires a literal 1,260 years; they reply with the day-year principle
Critics want a single controlling principle; eclectics answer that complex apocalyptic literature naturally works on several levels.
Which verse do some interpreters use to argue Revelation has past, present and future dimensions?
Revelation 1:19 (write the things seen, the things that are, and the things to come)
Dispensationalists read the verse as an outline (chapter 1; chapters 2-3; chapters 4-22); eclectics and Beale often read it as describing the mixed temporal scope of the whole book.
Is the eclectic approach tied to one millennial view?
Yes, only amillennialism
No; eclectic interpreters include amillennialists, premillennialists and postmillennialists
Yes, only dispensationalism
Yes, only full preterism
Beale is amillennial, Grant Osborne is premillennial, and some postmillennialists also blend preterist and idealist readings.
Which scholar's work on the theology of Revelation stresses its prophetic critique of Rome and its relevance as Christian prophecy?
Max King

Bauckham's The Theology of the Book of Revelation (1993) and The Climax of Prophecy highlight the book's Old Testament allusions and its critique of Roman power while affirming a future eschatological hope.
What is covenant theology?
A framework that organises Scripture around God's covenants, often summarised as covenants of redemption, works and grace, with strong continuity between Israel and the church
A system dividing history into seven dispensations
A form of full preterism
A Roman Catholic doctrine of sacraments
Covenant theology developed in the Reformed tradition (Zwingli, Bullinger, Cocceius, Witsius) and is expressed in the Westminster Confession chapter 7.
What is the 'covenant of grace' in covenant theology?
A covenant made with Adam before the fall requiring perfect obedience
A covenant between the Father and the Son in eternity
A covenant made only with the church after Pentecost
God's single gracious covenant of salvation through Christ, administered differently in the Old and New Testaments
The covenant of works was with Adam (Genesis 2:16-17; Romans 5:12-21), and the covenant of redemption is the intratrinitarian pact; the covenant of grace unites believers of all ages in Christ.
How does covenant theology generally relate Israel and the church?
As two peoples with separate destinies
As one people of God across both testaments, with the church as the continuation and fulfilment of Israel
As unrelated entities
As identical to modern national Israel

Texts such as Galatians 3:29, Galatians 6:16, Ephesians 2:11-22 and Romans 11's single olive tree are central; many covenant theologians still expect a future mass conversion of Jews (Romans 11:25-26).
Which millennial views are most common among covenant theologians?
Amillennialism and postmillennialism, with a minority of historic premillennialists
Vos, Hoekema and Riddlebarger are amillennial; Charles Hodge, Warfield, Bahnsen and Gentry are postmillennial; some Reformed thinkers, such as some Puritans, held premillennial views.
What do Reformed Baptists (1689 Federalism) differ on with Westminster covenant theology?
Whether Christ will return
Whether God made any covenants at all
Whether the Bible is inspired
Whether the new covenant includes believers' children, and so whether infants should be baptised

Paedobaptist covenant theology sees the sign of the covenant given to believers and their children (Genesis 17; Acts 2:39); 1689 Federalists see the new covenant as made only with the regenerate (Jeremiah 31:31-34).
What hermeneutical principle is typical of covenant theology?
The New Testament's use of the Old Testament guides interpretation, so Old Testament promises are read in light of their fulfilment in Christ
Old Testament promises must be fulfilled literally to national Israel
Only the Old Testament is authoritative
Prophecy should be interpreted using the day-year principle exclusively
Covenant theologians argue that Christ is the true Israel and seed of Abraham (Galatians 3:16), so promises such as the land find fulfilment in the new creation (Romans 4:13; Hebrews 11:16).
Which Princeton theologian is seen as a founder of Reformed biblical theology and the 'two-age' eschatological framework?
Joseph Mede
Vos's The Pauline Eschatology (1930) and Biblical Theology (1948) shaped later covenantal and amillennial thinking about the overlap of this age and the age to come.
What criticism do dispensationalists typically raise against covenant theology, and the reply?
That it denies the Trinity; they reply with the Nicene Creed
That it is too recent; they reply it dates from 1909
That it rejects Romans; they reply by rejecting Galatians
That it 'spiritualises' Old Testament promises to Israel; covenant theologians reply that the New Testament itself interprets those promises as fulfilled in Christ
Michael Vlach argues covenant theology is a form of 'replacement' theology; covenant theologians prefer 'fulfilment' and stress that Gentiles are grafted into Israel, not replacing it.
What is a 'dispensation' in dispensational theology?
A distinct stewardship or administration of God's dealings with humanity in history (from Greek oikonomia)
A period of exactly one thousand years
A spiritual gift given to the church
A Catholic indulgence
Ephesians 1:10 and 3:2 use oikonomia; Scofield described seven dispensations (innocence, conscience, human government, promise, law, grace, kingdom).
What were Charles Ryrie's three 'sine qua non' of dispensationalism (Dispensationalism Today, 1965)?
Seven dispensations, a pretribulational rapture, and a pre-70 Revelation
The covenant of works, covenant of grace and covenant of redemption
A consistent distinction between Israel and the church, consistently literal (normal) interpretation, and God's glory as the ultimate purpose of history
Historicism, idealism and futurism
Ryrie argued these, not the number of dispensations, define the system; progressive dispensationalists have modified the first two.
Which order of historical development is correct?
Progressive, revised, classic
Classic (Darby, Scofield, Chafer), revised or normative (Ryrie, Walvoord, Pentecost), progressive (Blaising, Bock, Saucy)
Revised, classic, progressive
